title: Feelings in depth
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE DATIVE-SUBJECT FRAME is this module's spine, and the learner has met it twice already without its name. mne grústno, mne stráshno, mne skúchno, mne stýdno — the person feeling it stands in the DATIVE and the predicate is a bare word ending in -o, and there is no subject in the sentence at all. L1-M9's mne nrávitsya and L2-M1's mne núzhno are the same shape: what happens, happens TO you. Learn the one frame and seven feelings come with it.

English says "I am sad" — a subject, a verb and an adjective, and Russian drops all three. ya grústnyy is not a clumsier way of saying it: it is a different claim, that you are a gloomy person by nature rather than sad this afternoon. The -o word never agrees with anybody, because there is nobody for it to agree with; mne grústno is what a Russian says about this afternoon.

rad is a SHORT-FORM adjective, and it agrees with the speaker rather than staying flat: rad from a man, ráda from a woman, rády from a group. This is M3's soglásen a second time, and the pair is worth noticing because short forms are otherwise a corner of the grammar a learner can leave alone — these two, with L2's svobóden and zanyát, are very nearly the whole list.

chúvstvuyu sebyá takes an ADVERB and never an adjective: chúvstvuyu sebyá khoroshó, plókho, lúchshe. The sebyá is obligatory, and it is NOT the -sya of M1's odeváyus'. That -sya is a particle welded to the end of a verb; sebyá is a free word standing after it. This module shows both at once — bespokóyus' carries one, chúvstvuyu sebyá the other.

The whole family takes a past with no new tense: býlo for the plain past, stálo for the change into it. mne býlo stráshno is "I was frightened"; mne stálo stráshno is "I got frightened", the moment the fear arrived. Both are neuter -o forms agreeing with nothing, because the frame still has no subject for them to agree with.

words.note: The -o predicate for sadness. It does not agree with you and never changes: the person it happens to stands in the dative in front of it, mne grústno.

sentences.trap: There is no ya in it and no verb either. Adding them — ya grústnyy — turns a mood into a personality.
sentences.sound: mnye si-VOD-nya GRUS-na. The t of grústno is not pronounced, and sevódnya's d is said as a v.

variations.changed: a different person in the dative

mistake.why: grústnyy is a gloomy sort of person, which is not what today is about. The mood takes the dative frame: mne grústno.

sentences.usage: Answering kak delá honestly, without making a speech of it.
sentences.mnemonic: To me — sadly. No I, no am.

words.note: Fear in the dative frame. One word covers "it is frightening" and "I am scared"; which one it means is decided by whether a dative stands with it.

sentences.trap: býlo is neuter because there is nothing for it to agree with. A man does not say byl here and a woman does not say bylá.
sentences.sound: mnye BY-la STRASH-na. Both words lean on their first syllable and the line falls away.

mistake.why: Two mistakes at once: this frame has no subject for byl to agree with, and the person belongs in the dative. mne býlo stráshno.

sentences.usage: Telling a story that ended well — the fear is safely in the past.
sentences.mnemonic: Was frightening to me. Neuter, always.

words.note: Boredom in the same frame. Like stráshno it does double duty: with a dative it is your boredom, without one it is the thing that is dull.

sentences.trap: English splits "I am bored" from "it is boring" and Russian does not. The dative is the whole difference.
sentences.sound: mnye SKUSH-na DO-ma. skúchno is said with sh, not ch — one of the few words where that happens.

mistake.why: skúchnyy is a boring person — you have said you are dull company. mne skúchno is the state you are in.

sentences.usage: A Sunday afternoon with nothing in it.
sentences.mnemonic: Boring to me — the dative says whose boredom it is.

words.note: A short-form adjective agreeing with the speaker: rad from a man, ráda from a woman, rády from a group. Exactly M3's soglásen — that row has the shape.

sentences.trap: This one is NOT the dative frame. rad has a real subject, so ya stays and the ending moves instead.
sentences.sound: ya RAT, shto ty ZDYES. The d of rad is said as a t at the end of the word.

variations.changed: a group, and a polite you

mistake.why: rad is not an -o predicate and takes no dative. It agrees with whoever is glad: ya rad, ya ráda.

sentences.usage: Meeting someone at the door, or at the end of a long trip.
sentences.mnemonic: rad, ráda, rády — glad has a gender.

words.note: The verb for how you are, in body or in mood. It is never used alone: sebyá comes with it, and what follows is an adverb — khoroshó, plókho, lúchshe.
A free word meaning "self", the same for every person. It is not M1's welded-on -sya: that one is part of the verb, this one stands after it.

sentences.trap: khoroshó and not khoróshiy. The complement of this verb is an adverb, so no adjective ever lands here.
sentences.sound: ya CHUST-vu-yu si-BYA kha-ra-SHO. The first v of chúvstvuyu is silent — CHUST, not CHUVST.

mistake.why: Without sebyá the verb says your senses are sharp. Your own state needs the self: chúvstvuyu sebyá khoroshó.

sentences.usage: The answer a doctor is actually asking for.

words.note: "Became" — the change into a feeling, where býlo is the feeling itself. mne býlo spokóyno is how the evening was; mne stálo spokóyno is the moment it turned.
Calm, in the dative frame. It doubles as the ordinary adverb for doing a thing calmly, which is why it needs no second form.

sentences.trap: stálo is neuter and stays neuter, whoever is speaking. It has no subject to agree with.
sentences.sound: mnye STA-la spa-KOY-na. Three falling words; nothing here is stressed at the end.

variations.changed: a comparative in the same frame
a different person in the dative

mistake.why: stal wants a subject and an adjective after it. The feeling frame keeps the person in the dative and the verb neuter: mne stálo spokóyno.

sentences.usage: The moment after bad news turns out to be nothing.
sentences.mnemonic: Became calm to me — a past with no new tense.

words.note: A -sya verb, so the worrying stays with the worrier. The endings are M1's: -yus' for ya, -ish'sya for ty, -itsya for on and oná.
"About", and it takes the prepositional — the case L1-M7 opened for v and na. Before a vowel it is said and written ob: ob éhtom.

sentences.trap: Two selves in one module: bespokóyus' carries -sya welded to the verb, chúvstvuyu sebyá keeps sebyá free.
sentences.sound: ya bis-pa-KO-yus a ra-BO-tye. Unstressed o is said as a, so the preposition all but disappears.

mistake.why: o takes the prepositional, and rabóta becomes rabóte in it — the same ending you already say in na rabóte.

sentences.usage: Saying what is on your mind without dramatising it.
sentences.mnemonic: o plus the -e case: worried about work, rabóte.

words.note: Shame in the dative frame. Russians reach for it where English would say "sorry": it admits the fault rather than asking to be let off.

sentences.trap: The comma before chto is obligatory, as it has been since M3. Russian puts one in front of every chto clause.
sentences.sound: mnye STYD-na, shto ya a-PAZ-dy-va-yu. chto is said shto, as always.

variations.display: Mne stýdno, chto ya ne pomóg
variations.script: Мне стыдно, что я не помог
variations.cue: I'm ashamed that I didn't help

mistake.why: There is no such adjective for a person here. Shame is a state that happens to you: mne stýdno.

sentences.usage: Arriving late and saying so before anyone else does.
sentences.mnemonic: Shameful to me — the fault admitted, not excused.

sentences.cue: I feel hurt, and he's cheerful

words.note: The feeling of being treated unfairly — closer to "it stings" than to anger. English has no one word for it, which is why it earns the room.
The short form of L2-M3's vesyólyy, agreeing like rad: vésel, veselá, vésely. The short form is the mood now, the long one the character.

sentences.trap: a is the quiet contrast — "and meanwhile". It is not no, which would set the two halves against each other.
sentences.sound: mnye a-BID-na, a on VYE-sil. The a between them is unstressed and almost swallowed.

variations.cue: She feels hurt, and he's cheerful

mistake.why: obídnyy describes the remark, not the person stung by it. The feeling is mne obídno, and vésel is his mood rather than his nature.

sentences.usage: The half-complaint you make to a friend, not to the person who caused it.
sentences.mnemonic: It stings me — a, and he is fine.

words.note: The ty form of S05's verb, carrying L1's -esh' ending. sebyá does not change for person — only the verb in front of it does.

sentences.trap: lúchshe is an adverb here and needs no ending. There is no question word either: the voice rises, and that is the question.
sentences.sound: ty CHUST-vu-yesh si-BYA LUCH-she. Again no v in the first syllable.

mistake.why: Without sebyá you have asked whether their senses are sharper. Feeling better about yourself needs the self in it.

sentences.usage: Calling someone the day after they were ill.
sentences.mnemonic: Feeling yourself better? The self never leaves.

comprehensionPool.cue: I feel hurt, and he's cheerful
I'm glad everything is all right
